claims.text: The target material is polycrystalline bulk HfNbTaTiZr with typical processing defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed multi-fidelity model will integrate ideal-lattice computational data with experimental data.
The experimental training data include the effects of processing defects and 1 wt.% oxygen.
The multi-fidelity model will predict HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more accurately than traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The claimed accuracy advantage applies especially in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Defects and oxygen impurities act as scattering centers.
Defect and oxygen scattering modifies electron or phonon transport relative to a perfect crystal lattice.
The model will learn a mapping from defect or impurity concentration and temperature to conductivity deviations from ideal behavior.
Incorporating idealized simulations and real measurements will compensate for limitations of analytical models that assume defect-free conditions.
The analytical baseline assumes a defect-free crystalline lattice and does not account for 1 wt.% oxygen.
At cryogenic temperatures, the model will capture enhanced scattering caused by defects.
At elevated temperatures, the model will capture the combined effects of thermal vibrations and impurity scattering.
The proposed applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with defect populations and oxygen contamination similar to those in the characterized material.
Predictions may not be reliable for samples with substantially different impurity concentrations or microstructures.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement will depend on the quantity and quality of the multi-fidelity training data.
Nonlinear defect interactions or unanticipated impurity effects could add prediction uncertainty.
A held-out conductivity measurement at 300 K on the oxygen-containing specimen is proposed as a benchmark.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if the machine-learning model fails to reduce prediction error by more than approximately 10% relative to the analytical model in either temperature regime.
The hypothesis is also declared falsified if the perfect-crystal model is within 5% of the measured 300 K conductivity.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis is comparative—lower error for the ML model—but the falsification rule independently rejects it when the perfect-crystal model is within 5% of the 300 K measurement. A baseline error below 5% does not preclude the ML model from being still more accurate, so this condition does not logically falsify the stated comparative claim.
